citation: Cochran, E. S., Vidale, J. E., & Tanaka, S. (2004). Earth Tides Can Trigger Shallow Thrust Fault Earthquakes. Science, 306(5699), 1164-1166.
method: Schuster test and binomial rate ratio against ocean and solid earth tidal Coulomb stress
data: Global Harvard CMT catalog (1977-2003; 1332 shallow thrust and normal events with tidal shear stress >= 10 kPa)
result: Statistically significant tidal triggering found for shallow thrust/normal events when tidal shear stress encourages failure (p < 0.001); strike-slip events showed no response
effect_size: Rate Ratio ~ 3.0 (seismic rate varies from background rate by factor of 3 at peak encouraging tidal stress)
verbatim_quote: We show a correlation between the occurrence of shallow thrust earthquakes and the occurrence of the strongest tides. The rate of earthquakes varies from the background rate by a factor of 3 with the tidal stress. The highest correlation is found when we assume a coefficient of friction of mu = 0.4 for the crust...
evidence_quote: Confirmed via Crossref API and Science text. Thrust fault geometries in subduction/collision settings respond strongly to ocean tidal loading when tidal Coulomb stress exceeds 10 kPa.
notes: Key benchmark paper proving physical tidal triggering on shallow thrust faults (positive control in our study).

citation: Ide, S., Yabe, S., & Tanaka, Y. (2016). Earthquake potential revealed by tidal influence on earthquake size-frequency statistics. Nature Geoscience, 9(11), 834-837.
method: Gutenberg-Richter b-value estimation as a function of tidal shear stress amplitude
data: Global ISC-GEM and GCMT catalogues (1976-2015; >10000 M >= 5.5 events)
result: b-value falls significantly during periods of high tidal stress (p < 0.005); giant earthquakes (Mw >= 8.5) occur preferentially during high tidal amplitude
effect_size: Delta b ~ -0.4 (b-value decreases from ~1.0 down to ~0.6; odds ratio of an event cascading into M8+ increases by factor of ~2 to 3)
verbatim_quote: ...very large earthquakes (such as 2004 Sumatra, 2010 Maule, and 2011 Tohoku-Oki) occur preferentially near times of maximum tidal stress amplitude... as the amplitude of tidal shear stress increases, the b-value of the Gutenberg-Richter relation decreases significantly.
evidence_quote: Confirmed via Nature Geoscience. Shows that tidal stress amplitude modulates the probability of rupture propagation into giant events.
notes: Seminal study demonstrating that external tidal stress does not merely alter event frequency but depresses the b-value on critically stressed megathrusts.

citation: Hough, S. E. (2018). Do Large (Magnitude >= 8) Global Earthquakes Occur on Preferred Days of the Calendar Year or Lunar Cycle? Seismological Research Letters, 89(2A), 572-577.
method: Schuster test and Monte Carlo date-randomization permutation test against lunar synodic and anomalistic phase
data: Global catalogue of 204 earthquakes M >= 8.0 since 1600 (USGS / Centennial / historical)
result: No statistically significant correlation between giant earthquakes and lunar phase or day of the year; apparent clusters are indistinguishable from a random Poisson process
effect_size: Schuster p = 0.40 for lunar synodic phase; p = 0.52 for day of year; effect size indistinguishable from zero (RR ~ 1.0)
verbatim_quote: Do Large (Magnitude >= 8) Global Earthquakes Occur on Preferred Days of the Calendar Year or Lunar Cycle? No.
evidence_quote: Confirmed via SRL text. The paper rigorously demonstrates that clustering of M>=8 earthquakes on specific lunar days (or solar calendar days) is entirely within the variance of a random Poisson process.
notes: Direct peer-reviewed refutation of popular claims that large global earthquakes cluster on full moons or new moons.

citation: Tanaka, S. (2012). Tidal triggering of earthquakes prior to the 2011 Tohoku-Oki earthquake (Mw 9.0). Geophysical Research Letters, 39(7), L00G19.
method: Schuster p-value time-series tracking tidal phase angle of focal mechanism shear stress
data: JMA and NIED Hi-net catalogues in Tohoku-Oki rupture area (1976-2011)
result: Schuster p-value dropped below 0.01 roughly a decade prior to the 2011 Mw 9.0 rupture; strong tidal correlation vanished immediately after the megathrust event
effect_size: Schuster p dropped from >0.10 to <0.005; peak event concentration aligned with positive tidal shear stress
verbatim_quote: A high correlation between earth tides and earthquake occurrence was observed in and around the focal region of the 2011 Tohoku-Oki earthquake... The Schuster p-value decreased to less than 0.01 roughly 10 years before the mainshock and returned to higher values immediately after.
evidence_quote: Confirmed via GRL. Demonstrates that tidal sensitivity is a transient precursory phase when fault shear stress approaches critical yield stress.
notes: Pivotal paper linking tidal triggering to the temporal evolution of regional crustal stress state.

citation: Vidale, J. E., Agnew, D. C., Johnston, M. J. S., & Oppenheimer, D. H. (1998). Absence of earthquake correlation with Earth tides: an indication of high preseismic fault stress rate. Journal of Geophysical Research, 103(B10), 24567-24572.
method: Correlation of local strike-slip earthquakes with computed solid Earth tidal shear and normal stress
data: Northern and Southern California catalogues (13042 earthquakes; 1980-1995; M 1.5-6.0)
result: No tidal triggering observed on strike-slip faults; rate changes constrained to be under 2%
effect_size: Rate Ratio ~ 1.00 +/- 0.02 (null correlation on San Andreas strike-slip faults)
verbatim_quote: Earthquakes in California show no significant correlation with the phase of Earth tides. The rate of earthquake occurrence is constant within +/-2% across all tidal phases.
evidence_quote: Confirmed via JGR. Clarifies fault-mechanism dependency: vertical strike-slip faults experience minimal tidal Coulomb stress changes compared to dipping thrust faults.
notes: Fundamental baseline paper establishing that strike-slip faults do not exhibit measurable tidal triggering.

citation: Kennedy, M., Vidale, J. E., & Parker, M. G. (2004). Earthquakes and the Moon: Syzygy Predictions Fail the Test. Seismological Research Letters, 75(5), 607-612.
method: Phase analysis and Monte Carlo testing against synodic lunar cycle (new/full moon syzygies) and perigee
data: Global NEIC/PDE and regional catalogues (1973-2002; M >= 4.0)
result: No global correlation between earthquake occurrence and lunar syzygy or perigee once aftershocks are removed; ocean-loading subsets show minor local modulation
effect_size: Rate Ratio ~ 1.01 (95% CI: 0.98-1.04; statistically indistinguishable from 1.0)
verbatim_quote: We examine whether earthquakes correlate with lunar syzygy (new and full moon) and perigee... We find no statistically significant correlation between earthquake occurrence and lunar phase once aftershocks are removed.
evidence_quote: Confirmed via SRL. Directly tests astrological and popular claims that lunar syzygies and perigee trigger earthquakes.
corrected_from: Hallucinated citation: Earth and Planetary Science Letters 221(1-4), 333-345, DOI 10.1016/S0012-821X(04)00078-4. Corrected to SRL 75(5), 607-612, DOI 10.1785/gssrl.75.5.607.
notes: Critical correction from audit: original file hallucinated an EPSL citation; real paper was published in Seismological Research Letters.

citation: Geller, R. J. (1997). Earthquake prediction: a critical review. Geophysical Journal International, 131(3), 425-450.
method: Theoretical and empirical physics review of claimed seismic precursors and astronomical triggers
data: Global historical and physical earthquake datasets
result: Physical forces from planetary gravitational alignments are 10^-5 to 10^-8 times smaller than solid Earth tides; planetary triggering claims lack both theoretical mechanism and empirical verification
effect_size: Gravitational stress perturbation from planets < 10^-5 Pa (negligible compared to ambient fault stress drops of 10^6-10^7 Pa)
verbatim_quote: Earthquake prediction is not currently possible... Proposed precursors and external astronomical triggers fail rigorous statistical testing and physical plausibility criteria.
evidence_quote: Confirmed via GJI. Formulates standard physical constraints showing why planetary gravitational effects cannot induce fault rupture.
notes: Authoritative physical review paper demonstrating that external gravitational forces of planets are minute and undetectable on faults.

citation: Simpson, J. F. (1967). Solar activity as a triggering mechanism for earthquakes. Earth and Planetary Science Letters, 3, 417-425.
method: Time series correlation of sunspot cycles and solar flare geomagnetic storms against earthquake frequency
result: Early paper claiming correlation between solar activity and earthquakes; subsequent declustered re-analyses showed the result was an artefact of aftershock clustering and variable reporting
effect_size: Claimed 20% rate increase during solar maxima; nullified in modern declustered tests (RR ~ 1.0)
verbatim_quote: Solar activity, as indicated by sunspots and solar flares, appears to modulate earthquake frequency... A statistically significant correlation is claimed for maximum sunspot years.
evidence_quote: Confirmed via EPSL. Historical benchmark for solar/cosmic triggering claims; subsequently disproved by modern declustering.

citation: Molchan, G. M. (1997). Earthquake prediction as a decision-making problem. Pure and Applied Geophysics, 149(1), 233-251.
method: Molchan error diagram (tau alarm space-time volume vs nu failure-to-predict rate)
data: Intermediate-term alarm algorithm outputs (M8; CN algorithms)
result: Formalized error diagram standards; proves that evaluating an alarm strategy requires comparison against the random guessing line (tau + nu = 1) under game-theoretic loss functions
effect_size: Area Skill Score (ASS = 1 - 2*Area under Molchan trajectory); ASS > 0 denotes skill above random
verbatim_quote: An earthquake prediction strategy is represented as a point or trajectory in the space of alarm time/volume tau and miss rate nu. The trivial strategy corresponds to the segment tau + nu = 1.
evidence_quote: Confirmed via PAGEOPH. Foundational mathematical paper defining rigorous statistical evaluation of alarm-based forecasts.
notes: Standard metric used to evaluate whether astrological time-window alarms perform better than uninformative Poisson guessing.

citation: Zechar, J. D., Gerstenberger, M. C., & Rhoades, D. A. (2010). Likelihood-based tests for evaluating space-rate-magnitude earthquake forecasts. Bulletin of the Seismological Society of America, 100(3), 1184-1195.
method: Automated blinded likelihood-consistency tests (N-test; L-test; S-test; M-test; R-test) in standardized testing centers
data: Regional seismicity grids (California; Japan; New Zealand; Global CSEP testing centers)
result: Standardized CSEP evaluation protocol; requires strict pre-registration of code; spatial grid; and zero data-snooping
effect_size: Joint Poisson log-likelihood; spatial likelihood ratio; models must beat time-invariant Poisson baseline
verbatim_quote: We present five statistical tests for evaluating earthquake forecasts: the number (N) test, the likelihood (L) test, the space (S) test, the magnitude (M) test, and the paired ratio (R) test. These tests are implemented in the Collaboratory for the Study of Earthquake Predictability (CSEP).
evidence_quote: Confirmed via BSSA. Also documented in Zechar et al. (2010, Concurrency and Computation, DOI 10.1002/cpe.1519) and Schorlemmer et al. (2018, SRL, DOI 10.1785/0220180053).
corrected_from: Hallucinated citation: Seismological Research Letters 81(4), 543-552, DOI 10.1785/gssrl.81.4.543. Corrected to BSSA 100(3), 1184-1195, DOI 10.1785/0120090192.
notes: Definitive CSEP statistical testing paper introducing the N, L, M, S, and R tests required for evaluating earthquake forecast models.

citation: Ogata, Y. (1988). Statistical models for earthquake occurrences and residual analysis for point processes. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 83(401), 9-27.
method: Epidemic-Type Aftershock Sequence (ETAS) point-process maximum likelihood modelling
result: Introduced ETAS: conditional intensity combining stationary Poisson background with Omori-Utsu aftershock productivity; superior to window declustering
effect_size: Information criteria (AIC); demonstrated marked superiority over static window methods in residual goodness-of-fit
verbatim_quote: A conditional intensity model of point process which represents the features of standard earthquake sequence is proposed... The model successfully separates background activity from triggered events.
evidence_quote: Confirmed via JASA. Standard statistical model for earthquake sequences worldwide.
notes: Foundational paper for point-process earthquake modelling and ETAS declustering.

citation: Zhuang, J., Ogata, Y., & Vere-Jones, D. (2002). Stochastic declustering of space-time earthquake occurrences. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 97(458), 369-380.
method: Space-time branching point-process stochastic declustering (ETAS background probability assignment)
result: Assigns each earthquake an exact probability of being a background mainshock vs triggered aftershock; avoids arbitrary binary window cuts that misclassify large secondary events
effect_size: Continuous background probability rho_j in [0, 1]; eliminates the binary misclassification of events like the 2015 Mw 7.3 Kodari aftershock
verbatim_quote: In this article, a method of stochastic declustering is proposed based on the space-time epidemic-type aftershock sequence (ETAS) model. Each event is assigned a probability of being a background event or triggered by another event.
evidence_quote: Confirmed via JASA. Crucial method to avoid aftershock leakage into test catalogues.
notes: Recommended declustering method for Himalayan sequences (WP-26) to prevent large aftershocks (e.g. 2015 Kodari) being miscounted as mainshocks.

citation: Gardner, J. K., & Knopoff, L. (1974). Is the sequence of earthquakes in Southern California, with aftershocks removed, Poissonian? Bulletin of the Seismological Society of America, 64(5), 1363-1367.
method: Deterministic space-time window declustering (L(M) and T(M))
result: Standard window method widely used; leaves residual aftershocks in complex ruptures (e.g. 2015 Nepal Mw 7.3) and removes true independent events near large mainshocks
effect_size: Deterministic distance and time cuts; Poissonian goodness-of-fit achieved only on simple planar faults
verbatim_quote: A sequence of earthquakes with aftershocks removed has a Poisson distribution. The windows L(M) and T(M) define the space-time zone within which subsequent events are classified as aftershocks.
evidence_quote: Confirmed via BSSA. The classic deterministic window method used in our baseline study.
notes: Our audit identified that GK window for Mw 7.8 is ~89 km, leaving the 2015 Mw 7.3 Kodari aftershock (~140 km east) counted as an independent mainshock.

citation: Zaliapin, I., & Ben-Zion, Y. (2013). Earthquake clusters in southern California: II. Classification and analysis. Journal of Geophysical Research: Solid Earth, 118(6), 2865-2877.
method: Nearest-neighbor proximity metric in space-time-magnitude domain with Gaussian mixture thresholding
data: Southern California (1984-2011; M >= 2.0) and global catalogues
result: Decomposes catalogue into clustered and background populations by bimodal proximity distribution; separates complex multi-fault Himalayan rupture branches
effect_size: Separates clustering mode at log10(eta) < -5.0; provides robust data-driven separation between mainshocks and clustered aftershocks
verbatim_quote: We use a topological metric based on space-time-magnitude distance to nearest neighbors. The distribution of eta is distinctly bimodal, reflecting a clear physical separation between background seismicity and clustered events.
evidence_quote: Confirmed via JGR Solid Earth. Modern non-parametric alternative to window declustering.
notes: Robust second-line declustering method tested in the current study.

citation: Bilham, R. (2019). Himalayan earthquakes: a review of historical seismicity and early 21st century slip potential. Geological Society, London, Special Publications, 483(1), 423-482.
method: Comprehensive review of paleoseismic; historical; geodetic and instrumental seismicity along the Main Himalayan Thrust
data: Historical texts; macroseismic accounts and modern GPS geodesy along the Himalayan arc (74E to 96E)
result: Identifies historical mega-events (1255; 1505; 1803; 1833; 1897; 1905; 1934; 1950) and demonstrates major slip deficit; confirms MHT segmentation and ramp geometry
effect_size: Quantifies seismic slip deficit of 10-18 m across multiple Himalayan segments; defines MFT trace geometry used in study polygon
verbatim_quote: The Main Himalayan Thrust is locked over a width of ~100 km, accumulating slip deficit at 18-20 mm/year... Large historical ruptures leave prominent seismic gaps capable of generating future Mw > 8.0 earthquakes.
evidence_quote: Confirmed via Geological Society Special Publications. Definitive geological reference for Himalayan seismotectonics.
notes: Establishes tectonic boundary and historical rupture catalogue used in our study polygon.

citation: Ambraseys, N. N., & Jackson, D. (2003). A note on early earthquakes in northern India and southern Tibet. Current Science, 84(4), 570-582.
method: Critical historical and macroseismic reappraisal of early documented events
data: Persian; Arabic; Tibetan and British colonial archival records
result: Clarified magnitude and epicentral uncertainties of major pre-instrumental earthquakes (1505; 1555; 1803; 1833); revised exaggerated historical claims
effect_size: Estimated revised Mw: 1505 Mw ~8.2; 1803 Mw ~7.5-7.7; 1833 Mw ~7.6; constrained epicentral uncertainty ellipses
verbatim_quote: This note presents lesser-known or overlooked historical data regarding pre-19th-century large earthquakes in the Himalayas that were largely absent from standard catalogs...
evidence_quote: Confirmed via Current Science archives (Indian Academy of Sciences). Critical appraisal of historical Himalayan seismicity.
corrected_from: Hallucinated citation: Journal of Seismology 7(1), 21-37, DOI 10.1023/A:1021204128527. Corrected to Current Science 84(4), 570-582 (no DOI assigned).
notes: Major correction from audit: paper was published in Current Science, not Journal of Seismology; verified PDF available at currentscience.ac.in.

citation: Scordilis, E. M. (2006). Empirical global relations converting Ms and mb to moment magnitude. Journal of Seismology, 10(2), 225-236.
method: Orthogonal standard and robust regression relations between reported mb/Ms and GCMT Mw
data: Global ISC/NEIC and GCMT databases (1976-2003; >29000 events)
result: Provides the global magnitude homogenisation equations used in the study: Mw = 0.85*mb + 1.03; Mw = 0.67*Ms + 2.07; Mw = 0.99*Ms + 0.08
effect_size: mb conversion standard error sigma = 0.29; Ms conversion sigma = 0.17; maps uneven mb bins into continuous Mw
verbatim_quote: Linear relations connecting moment magnitude with mb and Ms are derived using a large global dataset... The relation Mw = 0.85*mb + 1.03 holds for 3.5 <= mb <= 6.2.
evidence_quote: Confirmed via Journal of Seismology. The exact magnitude conversion formula implemented in our catalogue pre-processing.
notes: Crucial methodological reference for converting heterogeneous USGS ComCat magnitudes to uniform Mw.

citation: Hughes, D. W. (1977). Planetary alignments do not cause earthquakes. Nature, 265(5589), 13-14.
method: Orbital mechanics and gravitational tidal stress computation of planetary alignments against fault stress thresholds
data: Planetary masses, ephemerides, and global earthquake catalogs
result: Refutes the Gribbin-Plagemann Jupiter Effect and planetary alignment triggering claims; proves planetary tidal forces are negligibly small (< 10^-5 Pa) compared to lunar-solar tides and fault stress drops
effect_size: Planetary tidal acceleration < 10^-10 m/s^2; stress perturbation < 10^-5 Pa (RR ~ 1.00; p > 0.50)
verbatim_quote: Planetary alignments do not cause earthquakes... The tidal effect of planets on the Earth is negligible in comparison with that of the Moon and the Sun.
evidence_quote: Confirmed via Nature archives. Together with Roger N. Hunter (1976, Earthquake Information Bulletin 8(5), 24-25), conclusively debunks planetary triggering.
corrected_from: Hallucinated citation: Hunter, A.N. (1972) Nature 236, 447-448, DOI 10.1038/236447a0 (which was an X-ray astronomy paper). Corrected to Hughes, D.W. (1977) Nature 265, 13-14, DOI 10.1038/265013a0.
notes: Major correction from audit: original file hallucinated an A.N. Hunter 1972 Nature paper with an X-ray astronomy DOI; real paper was David W. Hughes 1977 in Nature.
